title: Tsurezuregusa · Essays in Idleness
intro: Yoshida Kenkō was a Buddhist monk who never quite left the world. He took his vows around 1313, but he didn't go off to the mountains. He stayed in or near the capital, Kyoto, kept up with people at court, and was one of the leading poets of his day. He wrote most of this book around 1330.

It starts with him bored at his desk, writing down whatever comes into his head. What comes out are 243 short pieces, some just one sentence, some a few pages: death, love, houses, handwriting, drinking, the moon, and a priest who gets a pot stuck on his head.

He says the world is wonderful because nothing in it lasts. He says a man with no interest in love is missing something, and that desire is the one thing you should really be afraid of. He goes to the festival and watches the crowd instead of the parade. He never decides which side he's on, and he doesn't pretend to.
Each section has a plain English version first. Under "Dig deeper" you'll find the original Japanese with readings, a word-for-word translation, and notes.
